title: Suspense, curiosity, and surprise: How discourse structure influences the affective and cognitive processing of a story
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; title and indexed keywords (suspense, curiosity, surprise, order of events, narrative comprehension) show it tests how the order in which events are told shifts suspense, curiosity and surprise; effect sizes not available here.
why_for_us: Classic manipulation of telling order: the same notary-case facts can be ordered to produce suspense (show the risk first), curiosity (show the odd outcome first) or surprise (hide the key fact).

title: Event schemas, story schemas, and story grammars
finding: Proposes the structural-affect theory linking event structure (chronological order) vs discourse structure (order of presentation) to readers' affect and to intuitions of what counts as a story, and reports an experiment on story schemas (per authors).
why_for_us: Gives the vocabulary for planning each 60-90 s episode: decide per episode whether the date conflict is told in event order (suspense) or out of order (curiosity/surprise).

title: Suspense in the absence of uncertainty
finding: Three experiments: introducing an obstacle to a well-known outcome (e.g., Washington becoming president) slowed verification of that known fact (anomalous suspense); the effect persisted across a brief delay and disappeared once suspense was resolved (per authors).
why_for_us: Suspense survives even when notaries in the audience can guess the legal outcome of a documented case; what matters is a vivid obstacle in the moment.

title: The Nature of Narrative Suspense and the Problem of Rereading
venue: Routledge (book chapter, Suspense: Conceptualizations, Theoretical Analyses, and Empirical Explorations)
finding: Elaborates the structural-affect theory of suspense, reviews the empirical literature on narrative suspense against it, and addresses why rereaders still experience suspense (per author).
why_for_us: Useful summary of when re-watching a known case still works, relevant for recaps and for audiences who know how such notarial cases usually end.

title: Toward a general psychological model of tension and suspense
finding: Theoretical paper arguing that tension and suspense in music, film, literature and everyday life build on domain-general mechanisms of anticipation, prediction and uncertainty about outcomes the person cares about (per authors).
why_for_us: Supports the idea that a deadline, a missing draft and a contested date can generate the same tension as danger if the viewer cares about the outcome.

title: Inducing narrative tension in the viewer through suspense, surprise, and curiosity
finding: Experiment, N=94, four versions of one audiovisual story (suspense, surprise, curiosity structures plus a non-fiction version): fictional structures induced narrative tension (anticipations, diagnoses, retrospections, emotions); curiosity played a triggering and organizing role for suspense and surprise (per authors).
why_for_us: Start an episode with a curiosity hook (why two dates?) and let it feed suspense and surprise later; a documentary-style retelling alone produced a different, less tense response.

title: Attention, Blending, and Suspense in Classic and Experimental Film
finding: Cognitive-linguistic analysis of Hitchcock's claim that suspense arises when viewers hold privileged information about a forthcoming undesirable event and cannot intervene; frames suspense as information management and audience anticipation (per authors).
why_for_us: Theory behind 'show the audience the older draft before the notary sees it'; not an experimental test of the bomb-under-the-table claim.

title: Suspense and Surprise
finding: Formal model: suspense in a period is the variance of next-period beliefs, surprise is the distance between current and previous belief; derives optimal schedules for revealing information to maximize suspense or surprise, applied to mystery novels, game shows and sports (per authors).
why_for_us: Use as a design rule for an 8-episode reveal schedule: keep the 'who agreed to the date' question close to 50/50 and let each episode move belief a lot.

title: Re-Living Suspense: Emotional and Cognitive Responses During Repeated Exposure to Suspenseful Film
finding: Experiment, N=50, three viewings of suspenseful clips with SCL and ECG: self-reported suspense, arousal and skin conductance declined with repetition, while self-reported enjoyment did not differ significantly (per authors).
why_for_us: Re-used footage in recaps loses tension but not necessarily liking; keep recaps short and add one new fact each time.

title: Early Grade School Children's Liking of Script and Suspense Story Structures
finding: Experiment with kindergarten to 2nd-grade children: as predicted by structural-affect theory, suspense stories were liked more than mundane scripts and than scripts with added non-integrated exciting events (per authors).
why_for_us: Excitement must be integrated into the causal chain; a dramatic but irrelevant moment in the office will not add suspense.

title: “Run for it!”: Viewers’ participatory responses to film narratives.
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics Creativity and the Arts
finding: Two think-aloud experiments: viewers generated participatory responses (e.g., urging characters); when information about potential negative outcomes was provided rather than withheld, viewers produced more participatory responses during suspenseful excerpts (per authors).
why_for_us: Closest available test of the Hitchcock principle: telling viewers about the risk (e.g., the client's son may have pushed the date) before the character knows makes them mentally 'warn' the notary.

title: Generating predictive inferences while viewing a movie
finding: Two experiments with Moonraker: viewers were more likely to generate a specific prediction when visual and discourse support were present, and likelihood rose with multiple sources of support; they predicted spontaneously even without instructions (per authors).
why_for_us: Plant clues in two channels (a document on screen plus a line of dialogue) when you want notaries to anticipate; one channel only when you want ambiguity.

title: You look where I look! Effect of gaze cues on overt and covert attention in misdirection
finding: Magic-trick experiment: participants were significantly less likely to detect the to-be-concealed event when misdirection was supported by the magician's gaze (per authors).
why_for_us: In vertical video, the notary's gaze steers where viewers look; a fair clue (date on the draft) can be shown while the actor looks elsewhere.

title: Cognitive bias and the poetics of surprise
finding: Analysis of novels and films arguing that narratives exploit the 'curse of knowledge' bias to engineer twists that feel both surprising and, in hindsight, inevitable (per author).
why_for_us: Design the episode-8 reveal so that earlier details re-read as obvious once the answer is known; re-show them in the final episode.

title: Elements of Surprise: Our Mental Limits and the Satisfactions of Plot
finding: Book combining literary analysis with cognitive science, arguing that good surprises work by exploiting cognitive biases, mental shortcuts and quirks of memory (per publisher abstract).
why_for_us: Practical framework for fair-play twists in a documented-case reconstruction.

title: A sixth sense: Narrative experiences of stories with twist endings
finding: Two reading experiments (N=28 Japanese; N=36 English speakers, four stories): on first reading greater empathy and stronger expectations went with slower reading, on second reading with faster reading; responses reflect changes in surprise and empathy (per authors).
why_for_us: Twists engage most when viewers empathise with a character first; build sympathy for the elderly client before revealing who agreed to the date.

title: The Effect of Making a Prediction about the Outcome of a Consumption Experience on the Enjoyment of That Experience
finding: Four experiments: people who made predictions about uncertain events enjoyed watching them significantly less than those who did not, contrary to their own expectations; anticipated regret explained the effect and removing it eliminated the effect (per authors).
why_for_us: Asking notaries in captions or polls to 'guess who agreed to the date' may reduce enjoyment; test before using interactive prediction prompts.

title: Increased or reversed? The effect of surprise on hindsight bias depends on the hindsight component.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
finding: Experiments reconcile conflicting findings: the effect of surprising outcomes on hindsight bias depends on the component (memory distortion, inevitability, foreseeability), so surprise can increase some components and reverse others (per authors).
why_for_us: A very surprising reveal may feel 'inevitable' yet not 'foreseeable'; plant enough earlier cues for notaries to feel they could have spotted it.

title: Expecting a Surprise? The Effect of Expectations on Perceived Surprise in Stories
finding: Two experiments with short everyday scenarios: varying how much attention was drawn to the enabling conditions of a surprise ending changed how surprising participants found it (per authors).
why_for_us: Even mundane office events can be surprising; control surprise by how much you foreground the enabling condition (e.g., that a draft was emailed).

title: Suspense, Predictive Inference, and Emotion in Film Viewing
finding: Chapter on whether suspense films make viewers form explicit predictive inferences about outcomes, addressing controversy about the psychological status of viewer expectation (per authors).
why_for_us: Reminds writers that suspense may run on vague expectation rather than explicit guesses; do not over-explain alternatives.

title: Detecting deceptive behaviour after the fact
finding: Experiment, 54 groups of 4-6 friends with a secret saboteur: no one noticed the deception at the time, but once told a deception had occurred participants identified the saboteur with substantial accuracy; interrogation did not improve accuracy (per authors).
why_for_us: Strong basis for a fraud-detection reveal: once the notary learns a document was falsified, re-reading earlier scenes lets viewers 'find' the deceiver themselves.

title: Surprise versus suspense in the production of stress reaction.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Film experiment: versions with 20-30 s of clue-furnishing anticipation before accidents produced higher autonomic stress than 'surprise' versions without warning, and most of the stress occurred during the anticipation period (per authors).
why_for_us: Twenty to thirty seconds of foreseen threat fits a 60-90 s episode; show the deadline approaching rather than cutting straight to the outcome.

title: The role of temporal expectancies in the production of film suspense
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; indexed keywords (temporal expectancy, temporal predictability, temporal contrast) indicate it studies how expectations about when an outcome will arrive shape film suspense; results not verifiable here.
why_for_us: Relevant to the Tuesday 11:30 deadline: viewers' sense of when the outcome is due is itself a suspense lever.

title: Outcome value and outcome delay as determinant factors of suspense in film viewing: an experiment
finding: Experiment, N=124, 2 (outcome value) x 2 (outcome delay) between subjects x 4 genres: film suspense depended on both what is at stake and how long the outcome is delayed (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: Delay the answer to the date question while keeping stakes visible; both factors matter.

title: Can't finish what you started? The effect of climactic interruption on behavior
finding: Experiments: interruptions at climactic moments of an activity heightened the need for psychological closure, and the unmet need led people to seek closure in unrelated domains (per authors).
why_for_us: Cutting an episode at its climax creates a closure need; give a small closure (one fact settled) so viewers do not drift to other content.

title: The effect of suspense structure on felt suspense and narrative absorption in literature and film
finding: Online experiment, 2 (film vs literature) x 2 (diegetic vs non-diegetic delay) x 2 stories: non-diegetic delay (interrupting the story from outside) decreased felt suspense and absorption regardless of medium; attention was central to felt suspense (per authors).
why_for_us: Delay the outcome inside the story world (a phone rings, the son arrives) rather than with title cards or narrator asides.

title: Development of story liking: Character identification, suspense, and outcome resolution.
finding: Developmental model tested with suspense stories: identification rises with perceived similarity to the character, identification increases suspense, outcome liking depends jointly on character valence and outcome valence, and story liking rises with identification, suspense and outcome liking (per authors).
why_for_us: Make the notary similar to the notary audience (routines, vocabulary) to raise identification and thus suspense.

title: Does Entertainment Suffer From Interactivity? The Impact of Watching an Interactive TV Movie on Viewers' Experience of Entertainment
finding: Experiment, N=427, 3 interactivity levels x 2 introductions manipulating sympathy for the protagonist: viewers with lesser cognitive capacity felt more empathy and suspense without interactivity, those with greater capacity benefited from influencing the plot (per authors).
why_for_us: Interactive 'choose what the notary does' features may suit only some viewers; default to passive viewing.

title: The effect of suspense and its resolution on the appreciation of dramatic presentations
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; indexed keywords (suspense, adventure fiction, heart rate, skin temperature, physiological arousal) indicate a physiological test of how suspense and its resolution affect appreciation; results not verifiable here.
why_for_us: Foundational Zillmann test that resolution quality shapes appreciation; check full text before citing numbers.

title: The Impact of Lie to Me on Viewers’ Actual Ability to Detect Deception
finding: Experiment, N=108: viewers of a Lie to Me episode were no better at telling truths from lies than controls but more often misjudged honest interviewees as deceptive, i.e., lower truth bias and lower accuracy (per authors).
why_for_us: A series about a notary detecting fraud should not teach 'body-language lie detection'; show document and procedure checks, which matches what notaries actually do.

title: Effects of Situational Variables on Judgments About Deception and Detection Accuracy
finding: Experiment, N=242: observers judged more statements as deceptive when the situation implied high gain for the speaker, low probability of detection and low cost of being caught (per authors).
why_for_us: Viewers' suspicion of the son can be raised by framing what he gains from the earlier date, before any behavioural cue.

title: Unconscious processes improve lie detection.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Five experiments: judges kept from consciously deliberating for a period detected deception more accurately than judges who judged immediately or deliberated (per authors).
why_for_us: Supports a beat where the notary 'sleeps on it' before spotting the inconsistency; note this effect has been debated and should be checked for replications.

title: When Narrative Transportation Narrows Attention: Changes in Attentional Focus During Suspenseful Film Viewing
finding: Three experiments with suspenseful film excerpts: during 'hot spots' emphasizing potential negative outcomes viewers missed more audio probes and responded more slowly than during 'cold spots' (per authors).
why_for_us: Probe-detection is a cheap way to test 60-90 s cuts; at hot spots, avoid placing important dialogue or captions viewers must process.

title: Neural evidence that suspense narrows attentional focus
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; indexed keywords (suspense, visual attention, attentional focus, film clips, default mode network) indicate fMRI evidence that suspense narrows attention; numbers not verifiable here.
why_for_us: Converging neural evidence for keeping the frame simple at suspense peaks in vertical video.

title: Reading a Suspenseful Literary Text Activates Brain Areas Related to Social Cognition and Predictive Inference
finding: fMRI while reading E.T.A. Hoffmann's The Sandman in short passages: passage-wise suspense ratings related to activation in medial frontal cortex, inferior frontal sulcus, lateral premotor and posterior temporal/temporo-parietal areas, linked to social cognition and predictive inference (per authors).
why_for_us: Suspense recruits mind-reading: plots about who wanted what (son, client, notary) are a natural fit.

title: The Coupled Brains of Captivated Audiences: An Investigation of the Collective Brain Dynamics of an Audience Watching a Suspenseful Film
finding: fMRI, N=494 viewers: dynamic inter-subject correlation of brain responses tracked continuous suspense ratings from an independent sample, especially in salience and higher-cognition regions (per authors).
why_for_us: Continuous rating sliders from a small panel are a valid proxy for collective engagement; use them to pre-test episodes.

title: Building blocks of suspense: subjective and physiological effects of narrative content and film music
finding: Between-subjects study (audio-video vs video-only vs audio-only) with continuous ratings, heart rate, pulse amplitude and skin conductance: self-report and physiology were largely dissociated; tense music alone induced felt suspense; audio-only produced the highest arousal; heart-rate deceleration followed salient narrative clues (per authors).
why_for_us: Many vertical videos are watched muted or with sound: test both; music can carry suspense even when plot clues are thin, but do not rely on it alone.

title: A model of suspense for narrative generation
venue: International Conference on Natural Language Generation
finding: Proposes a domain-independent model for tracking suspense across a story using learned narrative schemas, intended to predict suspense in story generation (per authors).
why_for_us: Could be used to score draft scripts for suspense curve before shooting.

title: Dramatis: A Computational Model of Suspense
finding: Computational model: suspense equals the audience's difficulty in generating a plan for the protagonist to avoid an impending negative outcome; three evaluations including comparison with human ratings (per authors).
why_for_us: Operational test for each episode: count the notary's visible escape routes (call the client, find the draft, postpone) and remove one per episode.

title: Creating Suspenseful Stories: Iterative Planning with Large Language Models
finding: Proposes an iterative-prompting planning method grounded in suspense theory, noting that state-of-the-art LLMs are unreliable at generating suspenseful stories without such planning (per authors).
why_for_us: If AI tools help draft scripts, plan suspense explicitly (threat, escape options) rather than asking for 'a suspenseful scene'.

title: How It Ends: Exploring How Narrative Closure and Character Outcomes in Series Finales Relate to Viewer Responses and Coping Behaviors
finding: Online survey, N=840: positive main-character outcomes and perceived narrative closure were both associated with more positive and meaningful affect, less distress, and more enjoyment and appreciation of series finales (per author; correlational).
why_for_us: Episode 8 should give a clear answer to 'who agreed to the date' and a good outcome for the notary; an open finale is not supported.

title: The effect of information gap and uncertainty on curiosity and its resolution
finding: Missing-letters experiments: both size of the information gap and uncertainty predicted curiosity; later satisfaction depended on gap size, familiarity and whether participants had guessed correctly (per authors).
why_for_us: Each episode should leave a gap of moderate size and occasionally let viewers guess right, which raises satisfaction with the answer.

title: When No News Is Good News: Inferring Closure for News Issues
finding: Survey, N=264: people inferred a resolution for unresolved news stories, especially when less involved, and tended to infer that the issue had improved (per author).
why_for_us: Viewers who drop off mid-season may assume a happy resolution; recap the open question at the start of each episode.

title: Close Encounters of Two Kinds: False Alarms and Dashed Hopes
finding: Survey plus several experiments (incl. real-money coin tosses): when an initial event is unexpectedly reversed back to the starting state, the sequence feels better if the first event was a loss (false alarm) than a gain (dashed hope), and elapsed time between events moderates this (per authors).
why_for_us: Order of partial answers matters: a false alarm that resolves (deed looks invalid, then is saved) ends better than raised hopes that are dashed.

title: Questioning the end effect: Endings are not inherently over-weighted in retrospective evaluations of experiences.
finding: Experiments indicate that final moments are not inherently over-weighted in retrospective evaluations of hedonic experiences, contrary to the end-effect claim (per authors).
why_for_us: Do not rely on a strong last scene to rescue a weak episode; the whole 60-90 s counts.

title: Enjoying the possibility of defeat: Outcome uncertainty, suspense, and intrinsic motivation
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; indexed keywords (outcome uncertainty, suspense, intrinsic motivation, enjoyment, competitive games) indicate that uncertainty about winning raised suspense and enjoyment in competitive games; numbers not verifiable here.
why_for_us: Supports suspense from non-violent stakes: the chance the notarial act fails can be enjoyable tension.

title: Experimental Evidence for Suspense as Determinant of Video Game Enjoyment
finding: Experiment, N=63: a first-person shooter manipulated for low vs high suspense; results support suspense as a driver of enjoyment (per authors).
why_for_us: Further causal evidence that raising suspense raises enjoyment, though in a violent game context.

title: Positive Parasocial Relationships with Drivers Affect Suspense in Racing Sport Spectators
finding: Survey with structural equation model (Formula 1 viewers): positive parasocial relationships with a favourite driver raised suspense, while negative relationships to a disliked driver raised hopes for his failure but did not add suspense (per authors).
why_for_us: Suspense comes from caring about the notary or client, not from disliking the son; invest in a liked character.

title: Reconceptualizing and Reexamining Suspense as a Predictor of Mediated Sports Enjoyment
finding: N=161 viewers of one of 7 basketball games: a measure of the unfolding nature of suspense predicted enjoyment better than earlier final-score measures (per authors).
why_for_us: Measure and design the moment-to-moment course of tension, not just the outcome.

title: “BUZZER BEATERS” AND “BARN BURNERS”: THE EFFECTS ON ENJOYMENT OF WATCHING THE GAME GO “DOWN TO THE WIRE”
venue: Journal of Sport and Social Issues
finding: 2x2x2 experiment with an edited high-school football broadcast: the suspenseful version was more enjoyable and exciting, viewers cared more about the result; favourable outcomes were enjoyed more than unfavourable (per authors).
why_for_us: A deadline that goes 'down to the wire' (signing at 11:29) is enjoyable in non-violent contexts, especially with a favourable outcome.

title: When the Stakes are Low: How Key Features of Momentary Suspense Contribute to a Global Evaluation of Enjoyment
finding: Experiments with moment-to-moment suspense ratings for low-stakes competitions: more outcome uncertainty predicted total suspense and its slope, end, peak and time-to-peak; enjoyment correlated more with peak than with total suspense (per authors).
why_for_us: Low-stakes office suspense works if each episode has one clear peak; aim for a peak, not constant tension.

title: Do TV Viewers Value Uncertainty of Outcome? Evidence from the Australian Football League
finding: Observational analysis of TV ratings: higher match uncertainty was strongly associated with greater audience demand after controls (per authors).
why_for_us: Field evidence that uncertain outcomes attract audiences; keep the outcome of the documented case genuinely uncertain until late.

title: Experience, learning and the detection of deception
finding: Observational analysis of a TV game show in which decision-makers repeatedly identified a real person among impostors: evidence of learning, suggesting experience aids deception detection (per authors).
why_for_us: Impostor identification is a proven TV format; a notary's experience-based spotting of an impersonator is credible and watchable.
